ocar.opportunity: Correlated light and electron microscopy can pair functional and molecular labels with synaptic anatomy, but targeting EM to optically characterized cells without compromising high-throughput reconstruction remains hard.
ocar.challenge: CLEM often trades staining quality or throughput for registration, and thin neurites that are not attached to nearby large processes, myelin, or cell bodies force inefficient leapfrogging through dense optical features.
ocar.action: Friedrichsen, Ramakrishna, Hsiang, Valkova, Kerschensteiner, and Morgan, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2022), describe mrCLEM: ATUM sections on solid substrate are imaged repeatedly by SEM at multiple scales and matched to multiresolution confocal maps of aldehyde-fixed tissue, from gross anatomy down to subcellular features, to target high-resolution acquisition and annotation.
ocar.resolution: Features visible in lower-resolution EM correspond well to densely labeled optical maps, so iterative matching can aim high-resolution EM at cells of interest. They walk through a mouse retinal light-to-EM experiment and give examples from mouse brain slices. ATUM/SEM is highlighted because sections can be reimaged without distortion and modern SEMs switch between millimeter fields and nanometer resolution.
ocar.future_work: The authors flag that efficiency falls if hundreds of fine neurites must be traced without easy medium-to-high-resolution links; in those cases label-matching CLEM (NIRB or peroxidase) may be cheaper. They argue terabyte-scale volumes should be routinely paired with other modalities rather than waiting only for petabyte complete maps.

summaries.beginner: Light microscopy can show which cells are active or labeled, but electron microscopy is needed to see their synapses. This team images the same mouse tissue at several zoom levels so they only spend high-resolution EM time on the cells they already know from light.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2022), Friedrichsen and colleagues present mrCLEM, a multiresolution correlated light and electron microscopy pipeline built on ATUM/SEM. Arrays of sections on solid substrate are reimaged at multiple SEM scales and matched to multiresolution confocal maps of aldehyde-fixed tissue, from gross anatomy to subcellular landmarks, to target high-resolution acquisition. A mouse retina light-to-EM walkthrough and mouse brain-slice examples illustrate the link from live optical imaging to EM reconstruction. The discussion stresses that ATUM sections can be reimaged without distortion and that SEM can jump from millimeter overviews (cell bodies resolved) to nanometer fields.
summaries.advanced: The paper is a methods walkthrough rather than a completed dense connectome; imaging parameters are presented as a range of scales, not a single recommended setting. The main stated limit is fine neurites unconnected to nearby large structures, where leapfrogging through dense optical labels reduces the advantage over dense reconstruction. Comparison with NIRB or peroxidase CLEM is qualitative. Discussion does not quantify wall-clock savings, reconstruction completeness, or synapse-detection accuracy.

plain_language_summary: Light microscopy can show which cells are active or labeled, but electron microscopy is needed to see their synapses. This team images the same mouse tissue at several zoom levels so they only spend high-resolution EM time on the cells they already know from light.

ocar.opportunity: A full description of how neurons and brain regions interconnect is needed for mechanistic accounts of human brain function and dysfunction.
ocar.challenge: Diffusion MRI tractography maps whole-brain pathways at coarse scale, while polarization, fluorescence, and electron microscopy reach axons or synapses but not whole-brain coverage, so the scales are hard to combine.
ocar.action: Axer and Amunts, in Science (2022), review how to constrain whole-brain tractography with regional high-resolution connectivity and local fiber geometry, and they discuss machine learning and simulation where measurements are missing.
ocar.resolution: They argue that future interoperable atlases need high-resolution templates and directionality so that alternative tractography solutions and accuracy estimates can be represented together.
ocar.future_work: The review frames new methods, templates, and uncertainty-aware atlases as mandatory rather than reporting a single completed multi-scale human connectome.

summaries.beginner: Human brain wiring can be mapped with MRI of the whole brain or with microscopes that see single axons, but those views live at very different zoom levels. This Science piece argues we need ways to combine them, and to show how sure we are about each pathway.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2022), Axer and Amunts review the nested human connectome across diffusion MRI tractography and higher-resolution polarization, fluorescence, and electron microscopy. They argue that whole-brain tractography must be informed and constrained by regional connectivity and local fiber geometry, with machine learning and simulation filling gaps. Future interoperable atlases, they write, should include high-resolution templates, directionality, variant tractography solutions, and estimates of accuracy.
summaries.advanced: The associated PDF extract is a different paper: Schilling et al., Clinical Neuroradiology (2026), on unimodal versus multimodal XTRACT reconstruction of language-related white-matter tracts in 20 healthy adults, not Axer and Amunts on nested human connectomes. This card uses only the catalog abstract. The review itself is conceptual; it does not report new empirical multi-scale reconstructions or quantitative atlas accuracy.

plain_language_summary: Human brain wiring can be mapped with MRI of the whole brain or with microscopes that see single axons, but those views live at very different zoom levels. This Science piece argues we need ways to combine them, and to show how sure we are about each pathway.

ocar.opportunity: Fast cholinergic transmission is well mapped onto excitatory nicotinic receptors, but inhibitory acetylcholine-gated channels in invertebrates, and their circuit roles, are much less understood.
ocar.challenge: C. elegans has a large, partly orphan ligand-gated ion channel repertoire, and a compact nervous system in which the same neuron may mix excitatory and inhibitory receptors for a given transmitter.
ocar.action: Hardege, Morud, Courtney, and Schafer, in Journal of Neuroscience (2023), characterize new inhibitory channels in C. elegans, including choline-preferring LGC-40, LGC-57, and LGC-58 and polymodal LGC-39, then use ligand–receptor pairs to predict synaptic polarity across the hermaphrodite connectome.
ocar.resolution: They report that many neurons express both excitatory and inhibitory channels for acetylcholine and other major transmitters, and they present a polarity model intended to generate circuit hypotheses. GFP tagging of LGC-40, LGC-57, and LGC-58 is stated not to change EC50 in oocyte dose–response curves.
ocar.future_work: The polarity heatmap is a summed-expression model, not a measured sign at each synapse, so circuit tests of predicted excitation versus inhibition remain to be done.

summaries.beginner: In the worm, acetylcholine is not only an on-switch: some newly characterized channels prefer choline and can turn cells down instead of up. The authors use those receptors to guess which connections in the wiring diagram are excitatory or inhibitory.
summaries.intermediate: Published as an early-release article in Journal of Neuroscience (2023; DOI 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1516-22.2022), Hardege and colleagues identify inhibitory acetylcholine-gated channels in C. elegans, including choline-preferring LGC-40, LGC-57, and LGC-58 and polymodal LGC-39, activated by cholinergic and aminergic ligands. Using new ligand–receptor pairs they argue that single hermaphrodite neurons often co-express excitatory and inhibitory channels for acetylcholine, glutamate, and GABA. They build a model of synaptic polarity across the connectome as a hypothesis generator. Figure legends in the extract describe oocyte dose–response traces, antagonist applications, and a binary polarity heatmap.
summaries.advanced: The PDF extract is the correct paper but is badly encoded, so quantitative claims are taken from the abstract and readable figure legends rather than a recovered Discussion. Polarity is inferred from summed LGIC expression per neural class, not from paired physiology at identified synapses. Catalog year is 2021; the journal cites 2023. Still-orphan LGICs (LGC-42, -44, -45, -47, -48) appear in co-expression traces with RIC-3 and are not fully deorphanized here.

plain_language_summary: In the worm, acetylcholine is not only an on-switch: some newly characterized channels prefer choline and can turn cells down instead of up. The authors use those receptors to guess which connections in the wiring diagram are excitatory or inhibitory.

ocar.opportunity: Urgent actions such as defensive escape must pick a left or right trajectory immediately, so directionality may be implemented in local spinal circuits rather than only in higher cognition.
ocar.challenge: Brainstem Mauthner cells can fire bilaterally, so escape direction may be set downstream in the spinal cord; the identity and role of the relevant descending interneurons had been unclear.
ocar.action: Guan, Xu, Zhang, Huang, Wang, Dahlberg, Wang, Wang, Pallucchi, Hua, El Manira, and Song, in PNAS (2021), combine electrophysiology, serial block-face electron microscopy, and behavior in adult zebrafish to reconstruct a spinal circuit built around segmentally repeating cholinergic V2a (Chx10) interneurons.
ocar.resolution: These cells amplify brainstem escape commands and deliver excitation via a feedforward, axo-axonic circuit to fast motor neurons and commissural interneurons. Unilateral ablation of the cholinergic V2a cells eliminated escape-command propagation. The authors conclude that local spinal circuits can implement directionality of urgent motor actions.
ocar.future_work: How this specialized escape module interacts with swimming V2a modules, and whether homologous axo-axonic hubs exist in other vertebrates, is left open.

summaries.beginner: When a fish must dart left or right to escape, the spinal cord—not only the brain—helps choose the side. This study finds a repeating class of spinal cells that amplify the brain’s escape command and send it straight to motor neurons via axon-to-axon synapses.
summaries.intermediate: Published in PNAS (2021), Guan and colleagues map a specialized adult zebrafish spinal circuit for escape direction. A unique class of segmentally repeating cholinergic V2a interneurons expressing Chx10 amplifies brainstem commands and, through fast axo-axonic synapses that bypass soma and dendrites, drives fast motor neurons and commissural interneurons. Combining electrophysiology, serial block-face EM, and behavior, they report that unilateral ablation of these cells stops escape-command propagation. The significance statement frames this as a full functional connectome of the hub circuit.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text captures the abstract, significance, and introduction plus the reference list, not a full Discussion, so ablation and axo-axonic claims are those stated up front. “Full functional connectome” refers to this specialized escape module, not the entire spinal cord. Adult zebrafish is the experimental system; homology to goldfish spinal descending interneurons is discussed as background. Escape directionality is the assayed behavior, not general locomotion.

plain_language_summary: When a fish must dart left or right to escape, the spinal cord—not only the brain—helps choose the side. This study finds a repeating class of spinal cells that amplify the brain’s escape command and send it straight to motor neurons via axon-to-axon synapses.

ocar.opportunity: Individual neurons are well characterized, but brains compute through synaptic patterns; a shared vocabulary of motifs and larger architectures would bridge single cells and whole-brain function.
ocar.challenge: Circuit organization looks heterogeneous across regions and species, and unlike engineered computers, neuronal circuits arise from evolution and development rather than top-down design.
ocar.action: Luo, in Science (2021), reviews core motifs (feedforward and feedback excitation and inhibition, lateral and mutual inhibition) and larger plans (topographic maps, parallel processing, dimensionality expansion, biased neuromodulatory projections, recurrent loops), plus how they assemble in development and evolution.
ocar.resolution: The review treats motifs as “words” and architectural plans as “sentences,” arguing that these patterns implement elementary computations and specialized functions across diverse brains, and that molecular gradients versus combinatorial surface codes can specify maps versus discrete parallel pathways.
ocar.future_work: Luo calls for serial EM and trans-synaptic tracing across species, functional perturbation of key elements, and study of how motifs interact across scales; whether algorithmic changes in wiring explain mammalian complexity remains unknown.

summaries.beginner: Brain cells do not work alone: they are wired into repeating patterns, like feedforward loops and maps of neighboring cells. This review collects those patterns and asks how they are built in development and evolution.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Science (2021), Luo reviews neuronal circuit architectures from microcircuit motifs to larger-scale plans. Motifs include feedforward excitation and inhibition, feedback inhibition, lateral inhibition, and mutual inhibition; larger plans include continuous topographic mapping, discrete parallel processing, dimensionality expansion, biased neuromodulatory projections, and recurrent loops. He discusses conservation versus independent evolution, duplication and divergence, and developmental specification by molecular gradients versus combinatorial cell-surface codes. The outlook urges serial EM, trans-synaptic tracing, and cross-scale functional tests, including inspiration for artificial networks.
summaries.advanced: This is a synthesis, not new connectomic data. Motifs are illustrated rather than quantified across a defined corpus of circuits. The human-brain scale (“about 100 billion neurons”) is background context. Claims about AI inspiration and general-purpose networks are prospective. The extract’s Outlook notes that we still do not know whether algorithmic changes in wiring account for mammalian complexity.

plain_language_summary: Brain cells do not work alone: they are wired into repeating patterns, like feedforward loops and maps of neighboring cells. This review collects those patterns and asks how they are built in development and evolution.

ocar.opportunity: Nematode function is usually read from the synaptic connectome, but extrasynaptic volume transmission could let peptides act far from their release sites, including on reproductive muscle.
ocar.challenge: In Ascaris suum, FLP-18 peptides strongly affect female reproductive organs yet are expressed in cells with no known synapses onto that tissue, and body-cavity fluid had not been shown to carry nematode neuropeptides.
ocar.action: Atkinson, Liu, McKay, Vandewyer, Viau, Irvine, Rosa, Li, Liang, Marks, Maule, Mitreva, Beets, Li, and Mousley, in ACS Chemical Neuroscience (2021), profile A. suum pseudocoelomic fluid (As-PCF), test it on muscle and C. elegans FLP-18 receptors, and survey FLP-18 pathway conservation.
ocar.resolution: As-PCF contains a neuropeptide catalog dominated by As-FLP-18A, modulates nematode reproductive muscle ex vivo like synthetic FLP-18, activates C. elegans NPR-4 and NPR-5, and alters C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 and its receptors show pan-phylum nematode distribution. The authors present this as direct evidence for extrasynaptic peptide volume transmission.
ocar.future_work: How much EVT reshapes “functional connectome” models used in anthelmintic receptor deorphanization is posed as a drug-discovery implication rather than a completed network rewrite.

summaries.beginner: Worm wiring diagrams show synapses, but chemical messages can also travel in the body fluid. This study finds a peptide in the pig-parasite worm’s body fluid that can reach reproductive muscle even without a direct synaptic connection.
summaries.intermediate: Published in ACS Chemical Neuroscience (2021), Atkinson and colleagues test extrasynaptic volume transmission in nematodes using Ascaris suum pseudocoelomic fluid. Mass spectrometry shows a neuropeptide catalog in which As-FLP-18A dominates; the fluid modulates reproductive muscle ex vivo like synthetic FLP-18 peptides, activates C. elegans FLP-18 receptors NPR-4 and NPR-5, and changes C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 and receptors are reported as pan-phylum in nematodes. The paper positions EVT as a nonsynaptic route that matters for receptor deorphanization and pathogen drug discovery.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF text is dominated by publisher front matter and the reference list; quantitative peptidomics counts and potency values are not recovered beyond the abstract. Evidence is pharmacological and biochemical (fluid contents, ex vivo muscle, heterologous receptors, behavior), not EM of extrasynaptic release. Dominance of As-FLP-18A is stated without a numeric fraction in the extract. Cross-species receptor activation does not by itself prove in vivo volume transmission in C. elegans.

plain_language_summary: Worm wiring diagrams show synapses, but chemical messages can also travel in the body fluid. This study finds a peptide in the pig-parasite worm’s body fluid that can reach reproductive muscle even without a direct synaptic connection.

ocar.opportunity: Direction selectivity is a classic retinal computation in non-primate mammals, but whether primate retina computes motion direction—or cortex replaced that need—has remained open.
ocar.challenge: Starburst amacrine cells exist in primates, yet their wiring was unknown, primate direction-selective ganglion cells had not been found, and electrophysiology is biased toward the few abundant RGC types.
ocar.action: Patterson, Bembry, Mazzeferri, Neitz, Rieke, Soetedjo, and Neitz, on bioRxiv (2021), reconstruct the ON SAC circuit from a serial EM volume of macaque central retina and ask which ganglion cells SACs target.
ocar.resolution: They report that the structural basis for SAC computation and conferral of directional selectivity is conserved, and that SACs selectively target a single ganglion cell type, a candidate homolog of mammalian ON-sustained dsRGCs that project to the accessory optic system and support gaze-stabilizing reflexes.
ocar.future_work: Physiological confirmation that the targeted RGC type is direction-selective, and how this ancestral circuit sits beside primate cortical motion processing, remain to be shown.

summaries.beginner: Other mammals compute motion direction in the retina; primates were thought to wait until visual cortex. This preprint reconstructs macaque retinal wiring and finds a conserved circuit that could compute direction much earlier than expected.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2021), Patterson and colleagues present a connectomic reconstruction of the primate ON starburst amacrine cell circuit from serial EM of macaque central retina. They argue the structural basis for SAC direction computation and selective inhibition of postsynaptic RGCs is conserved, and that SACs target a single ganglion cell type proposed as a homolog of ON-sustained dsRGCs projecting to the accessory optic system. The introduction frames the result against the idea that expanded primate cortex replaced retinal direction selectivity, versus a sampling bias that missed rare RGC types.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint; the selected extract does not include a Discussion section (it runs into methods references). Conservation is structural, not a demonstrated direction-selective spike train in the candidate RGC. “Selectively target a single ganglion cell type” is an authorship claim from the abstract. The volume is macaque central retina, not peripheral retina or human.

plain_language_summary: Other mammals compute motion direction in the retina; primates were thought to wait until visual cortex. This preprint reconstructs macaque retinal wiring and finds a conserved circuit that could compute direction much earlier than expected.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans produces forward and backward locomotion with only 69 motor neurons and 95 muscle cells, so a connectome-based model could test whether that sparse circuit can generate both gaits.
ocar.challenge: Prior models mapped connectome and cell-class roles but did not analyze the distribution of synaptic and gap-junction weights needed for switching oscillations.
ocar.action: Sakamoto, Soh, Suzuki, Iino, and Tsuji, in Scientific Reports (2021), build a network of A, B, D, and AS motor neurons plus muscle, including chemical and gap junctions, and train connection weights with backpropagation through time on command-neuron input and muscle activation.
ocar.resolution: The circuit generated oscillations with different phase patterns for forward and backward movement and could switch at arbitrary times given binary command-like inputs. Trained synaptic and gap weights followed a Boltzmann-type distribution. The model could be trained to match measured activity in the HRB4 strain. The conclusion stresses that sparse connection strengths suffice for the oscillations.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest the same supervised approach could analyze more complex measured activity patterns; the extract does not claim a unique biological weight set.

summaries.beginner: The tiny worm walks forward and backward with a small set of motor neurons. This team trains a wiring-based computer model until the virtual muscles oscillate in both directions and can switch when a command-like input flips.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Scientific Reports (2021), Sakamoto and colleagues present a connectome-based neuromuscular model of C. elegans including motor neuron classes A, B, D, and AS plus muscle, with synaptic and gap connections. Weights are trained by backpropagation through time on teacher data of command-neuron input and muscle activation. Simulations produced forward- and backward-phase oscillations switchable at arbitrary times, and trained weights followed a Boltzmann-type distribution. The model could reproduce measured activity in the HRB4 strain. The conclusion emphasizes that a motor neuron–muscle network with sparse connection strength can generate the oscillations.
summaries.advanced: Weights are learned, not measured synapses; a Boltzmann-type distribution is a fit to trained parameters. “Sparse” is qualitative in the conclusion. Switching uses binary inputs that simulate command neurons rather than reconstructed premotor dynamics. HRB4 matching is stated without error metrics in the extract. The model is the motor/muscle layer, not the full 302-neuron connectome.

plain_language_summary: The tiny worm walks forward and backward with a small set of motor neurons. This team trains a wiring-based computer model until the virtual muscles oscillate in both directions and can switch when a command-like input flips.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal prostheses stimulate surviving cells after photoreceptor loss, but current flow in early degenerating retina is poorly quantified, limiting stimulation design.
ocar.challenge: Remodeling can begin before substantial photoreceptor death, so healthy versus early-degenerate rod-to-rod-bipolar pathways may already differ in morphology and input count.
ocar.action: Kosta, Iseri, Loizos, Paknahad, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Anderson, Jones, and Lazzi, in Experimental Eye Research (2021), build conductance-based NEURON models from serial-section TEM connectomes of healthy (RC1) and early-degenerate (RPC1) rabbit retina.
ocar.resolution: Simulated RodBC membrane potential in early degenerate tissue was about 10–20 mV lower than in wild type, attributed primarily to fewer rod inputs rather than intrinsically different RodBC biophysics. Frequency-response and step analyses suggested individual RodBC responses do not differ significantly before substantial photoreceptor loss, though frequency-dependent impedances are reduced. Both circuits showed similar low-pass filtering.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the models as tools for later-stage degeneration and prosthesis research; later disease stages are not simulated here.

summaries.beginner: When the retina starts to degenerate, rod bipolar cells still look similar but they receive input from fewer rods. Computer models built from electron-microscope wiring diagrams predict those cells sit at a lower voltage, which matters for designing retinal implants.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Experimental Eye Research (2021), Kosta and colleagues compare current flow from rods to rod bipolar cells (RodBCs) using morphologically accurate models from 70 nm serial TEM of healthy rabbit connectome RC1 and early-degenerate pathoconnectome RPC1. Passive and active conductances are implemented in NEURON. Photocurrent input yielded RodBC membrane potentials about 10–20 mV lower in RPC1, explained mainly by reduced rod input rather than altered RodBC intrinsic properties. Frequency and step analyses found similar individual-cell responses and low-pass filtering, with reduced frequency-dependent impedances.
summaries.advanced: The 10–20 mV difference is a simulated range, not a measured intracellular value. “Do not differ significantly” refers to matched-input single-cell responses, not network output or prosthetic thresholds. Early-stage RPC1 is one pathoconnectome; later degeneration is out of scope. Parameter tables are referenced but not numerically reproduced in the extract.

plain_language_summary: When the retina starts to degenerate, rod bipolar cells still look similar but they receive input from fewer rods. Computer models built from electron-microscope wiring diagrams predict those cells sit at a lower voltage, which matters for designing retinal implants.

ocar.opportunity: Direction selectivity is well known in non-primate retina and in primate visual cortex, but had not been demonstrated in primate retina despite dedicated effort.
ocar.challenge: Primate ganglion cell type lists are shorter than in other mammals, so either DS types are missing or they were undersampled because gene reporters are lacking.
ocar.action: Kim, Peterson, Crook, Joo, Wu, Puller, Robinson, Gamlin, Yau, Viana, Troy, Smith, Packer, Detwiler, and Dacey, in Nature Communications (2022), combine light-evoked recordings with connectomic reconstruction in macaque retina.
ocar.resolution: They identify diverse direction-selective types, including an ON-OFF ganglion cell, a spiking ON-OFF polyaxonal amacrine cell, and the starburst amacrine cell. Macaque starbursts have a strong non-GABAergic antagonistic surround from excitatory bipolar cells that the authors say is critical for radial motion sensitivity.
ocar.future_work: The paper opens investigation of precortical primate motion circuitry; how these retinal signals map onto cortical motion areas is not resolved here.

summaries.beginner: Textbooks often say primates compute visual motion in cortex, not in the eye. This study records from macaque retina and traces its wiring, and finds cells that already prefer motion in particular directions.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Communications (2022), Kim and colleagues combine light-evoked physiology with connectomic reconstruction to identify direction-selective cell types in macaque retina. The circuitry includes an ON-OFF ganglion cell, a spiking ON-OFF polyaxonal amacrine, and starburst amacrine cells, all reported as direction-selective. They describe a strong non-GABAergic antagonistic surround in macaque starbursts, mediated by excitatory bipolar input and critical for radial motion sensitivity. The introduction contrasts this with prior failures to find primate retinal DS and with richer DS type lists in non-primate mammals.
summaries.advanced: The selected extract does not include the Discussion (it ends in references). Diversity of DS types is asserted without counts in the abstract. Catalog year is 2021; the article is 2022. The non-GABAergic surround mechanism is a central claim to check against full figures. Catalog organism tags include mouse; the study is macaque.

plain_language_summary: Textbooks often say primates compute visual motion in cortex, not in the eye. This study records from macaque retina and traces its wiring, and finds cells that already prefer motion in particular directions.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain synaptic maps are now technically discussed even for a mouse, so the field needs a clear account of what such a map can and cannot explain.
ocar.challenge: Grand projects tend to overpromise: horizontal results (a synapse map) are sold as vertical conclusions (function, behavior, mind), a move Gomez-Marin calls theoretically flawed.
ocar.action: Gomez-Marin, in eNeuro (2021), writes a commentary on Abbott et al. (2020), “The Mind of a Mouse,” contrasting what connectomics measures with what it claims, and criticizing “all details matter” omics as promissory materialism.
ocar.resolution: He argues that suggesting a mouse, human, or fly connectome will “give us the mind” conflates levels of analysis. Maps are useful, but infinite resolution can be worse than the territory, and large projects crowd out other questions. Neural connections are not a replacement for mind.
ocar.future_work: The piece asks for conceptually serious metaphors and hypothesis-led work rather than proposing an alternative mapping project.

summaries.beginner: Some neuroscientists talk as if a complete map of every synapse would explain a mouse’s mind. This commentary says a wiring diagram is still just a map of one level, not a theory of thought or behavior.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eNeuro (2021), Gomez-Marin critiques Abbott et al. (2020) on mapping a mouse brain at synapse resolution. He distinguishes horizontal results (synaptic connections) from vertical conclusions (function, behavior, cognition) and coins the problem as promisomics: overpromising omics. Quantity is illustrated with a Boston–Lisbon analogy for mouse versus worm connectome scale, but the qualitative objection is that distance does not reveal purpose. He warns that “all details matter” is a poor rationale when funding and attention are limited.
summaries.advanced: This is a commentary, not empirical connectomics. Engagement is with Abbott et al. (2020) and the White et al. (1986) “Mind of a Worm” heading, not a reanalysis of EM data. Claims about crowd-out of other projects are argumentative. The extract includes the author’s own earlier papers on necessity/sufficiency rhetoric; those are citations, not new experiments.

plain_language_summary: Some neuroscientists talk as if a complete map of every synapse would explain a mouse’s mind. This commentary says a wiring diagram is still just a map of one level, not a theory of thought or behavior.

ocar.opportunity: Questions about how circuits generate behavior are hard in mammals; a simpler, genetically tractable locomotor circuit could serve as a generic teaching and research model.
ocar.challenge: Mammalian networks are huge and poorly accessible, while fly work is often siloed from researchers who do not use Drosophila.
ocar.action: Hunter, Coulson, Zarin, and Baines, in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), review the Drosophila larval locomotor network centered on identified interneuron A27h, compare it to mammalian locomotor circuits, and discuss critical periods and interindividual variability.
ocar.resolution: They argue that TEM-based reconstructions already give a relatively complete A27h-related circuit (motor, inter, higher, and sensory neurons), with some synapses validated electrophysiologically, and that the fly toolkit plus optogenetics make this a rare experimentally useful model while the whole larval connectome is still unfinished.
ocar.future_work: The ultimate goal of a whole larval connectome is distinguished from the already usable A27h module as a model for mammalian circuit development and function.

summaries.beginner: Fruit-fly maggots crawl using a small, well-mapped set of nerve cells. This review explains why that crawling circuit is a good stand-in for studying how any motor circuit is built and how it can differ between individuals.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), Hunter and colleagues review the Drosophila larval locomotor circuit as a model for researchers outside the fly field. They focus on identified interneuron A27h and TEM reconstructions (Ohyama et al., 2015 and related work) linking A27h to motor, inter, higher, and sensory neurons, with some synapses validated by electrophysiology. Applications discussed include critical periods of development and interindividual circuit variability. The conclusion states that many neurons in this circuit can be manipulated with the Drosophila genetic toolkit, optogenetics, and electrophysiology.
summaries.advanced: This is a review of a still-partial larval connectome, not a new reconstruction. Completeness is claimed for the A27h-related circuit, with citations, not for the whole larva. Mammalian comparisons are analogical. Supplementary animation timing (4 s per segment versus ~1 s per stride) is pedagogical, not a new measurement.

plain_language_summary: Fruit-fly maggots crawl using a small, well-mapped set of nerve cells. This review explains why that crawling circuit is a good stand-in for studying how any motor circuit is built and how it can differ between individuals.

ocar.opportunity: The classic C. elegans connectome still guides circuit work, but new EM, computation, and single-cell methods have expanded synapses and molecular cell identity.
ocar.challenge: A fixed neuron count and wiring diagram can hide multifunctional cells and flexible use of hardwired circuits, including gut–brain signaling.
ocar.action: Byrd and Jin, in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), mini-review updated connectomics, progress toward a molecular atlas, locomotor-circuit tools (super-resolution, opto- and chemogenetics), and emerging neuro-gut findings.
ocar.resolution: They highlight previously unreported synaptic connections, network models of behavior, and cell-specific manipulation in behaving animals. Photoactivatable botulinum toxin is cited as conditionally and reversibly reducing thrashing under blue light with recovery after 24 hours in the dark. They conclude C. elegans still yields insight from microstructures to inter-tissue interactions.
ocar.future_work: The review points to further improvement of conditional tools and continued circuit dissection beyond locomotion, sensory, and memory topics covered elsewhere.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s wiring diagram is famous, but it is still being updated, and new genetic tools let researchers turn single cells on and off in a crawling animal. This short review collects those advances, including signals between gut and brain.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Byrd and Jin review recent C. elegans circuit work: re-examined connectomes that add previously unreported synapses, single-cell transcriptome maps, and cell-specific tools. They focus on the motor circuit and locomotion pattern generation, then touch the gut–brain axis. A cited proof-of-concept is photoactivatable botulinum toxin that reduced thrashing under blue light with recovery after 24 hours in the dark. Perspectives emphasize multifunctionality of identified neurons despite a fixed cell number.
summaries.advanced: This is a mini-review; new synapse counts are not given in the extract. The PA-BonNT thrashing result is cited as proof-of-concept, not generated here. Coverage of sensory and learning circuits is explicitly deferred to other reviews. Catalog spelling “Wired For Insight- Recent Advance” is the source title.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s wiring diagram is famous, but it is still being updated, and new genetic tools let researchers turn single cells on and off in a crawling animal. This short review collects those advances, including signals between gut and brain.

ocar.opportunity: Many networks can produce similar responses, so a method that names which synapses are required by a given function would turn activity into anatomical predictions.
ocar.challenge: Structure–function links are subtle: the same network can compute differently by context, and it is largely unknown which connection patterns are necessary for specific computations.
ocar.action: Biswas and Fitzgerald, in Physical Review Research (catalog year 2020), introduce a geometric framework for threshold-linear recurrent networks that, when the number of specified response patterns does not exceed the number of input synapses, calculates the solution space of feedforward and recurrent matrices consistent with those responses.
ocar.resolution: A noisy generalization shows the solution-space geometry can undergo topological transitions as allowed error grows. Certainty conditions are derived that guarantee a nonzero synapse between neurons, intended for application to neural activity data.
ocar.future_work: The framework is proposed for making rigorous anatomical predictions from activity under the model architecture; empirical tests on recorded circuits are not part of the abstract.

summaries.beginner: Lots of different wiring diagrams can make a network behave the same way. This theory paper describes a geometric test for when a synapse must exist if the network is to produce a given set of responses.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Physical Review Research (catalog 2020; DOI 10.1103/physrevresearch.4.023255), Biswas and Fitzgerald present a geometric framework for identifying synapses required by steady-state responses in recurrent threshold-linear networks. When specified patterns do not exceed the number of input synapses, they analytically compute the solution space of feedforward and recurrent connectivity. With noise, that space can change topology as allowed error increases. Certainty conditions guarantee a nonzero synapse, aimed at anatomical predictions from activity.
summaries.advanced: The associated PDF extract is a different paper: Galatopoulos et al., Nanomaterials (2020), on β-alanine surface treatment of Cu:NiOx hole-transporting layers in inverted perovskite solar cells (PCE up to 15.51%, heat lifetime up to 1000 h), not a neural-network geometry paper. This card uses only the catalog abstract. Assumptions (threshold-linear neurons, pattern count versus input synapses) bound the claimed uniqueness of synapses.

plain_language_summary: Lots of different wiring diagrams can make a network behave the same way. This theory paper describes a geometric test for when a synapse must exist if the network is to produce a given set of responses.

ocar.opportunity: Terabyte EM volumes hide patterns that are not known in advance, so an unsupervised embedding could let scientists query by example and cluster without labels.
ocar.challenge: Supervised detectors only find patterns they were trained for, and manual search of nano-scale volumes is intractable.
ocar.action: Huang, Yang, Takemura, Rivlin, and Plaza, on arXiv (2020), learn a latent representation with semantics-preserving augmentations so synthetic views of the same structure lie close in feature space, demonstrated on nano-scale EM including FlyEM-related data.
ocar.resolution: The representation supports query-by-example and clustering that correlates with biologically meaningful distinctions. They release a visualization tool and software ecosystem. Conclusions emphasize complementarity with supervised labels (e.g., clustering at predicted synapses; optional extra channels for boundaries and mitochondria).
ocar.future_work: They suggest using embeddings to seed training sets, initialize supervised models, and build cell-type hierarchies from features pooled on segmented neurons.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are too big to browse by hand. This method teaches a computer to group similar-looking bits of image so a scientist can click an interesting blob and find more like it.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on arXiv (2020; 2012.12175), Huang and colleagues train an unsupervised deep latent representation for massive EM volumes using augmentations that preserve semantic meaning. They demonstrate query-by-example and clustering aligned with biological distinctions, plus an interactive visualization stack. The conclusion argues the method is complementary to supervised work: embeddings can discover patterns, initialize training, and, if synapse or boundary predictions exist, cluster those locations or add them as extra channels.
summaries.advanced: The extract does not report numeric retrieval or clustering scores. Biological meaning of clusters is asserted qualitatively. EM examples are nano-scale animal brain tissue associated with Janelia FlyEM; the method is not a replacement for neuron segmentation. Pay-per-use BigQuery costs are mentioned as infrastructure, not a scientific result.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope stacks of brain tissue are too big to browse by hand. This method teaches a computer to group similar-looking bits of image so a scientist can click an interesting blob and find more like it.

ocar.opportunity: Microtubules follow neuronal morphology and could guide proofreading and subcompartment labels, but they are impractical to trace by hand in large EM volumes.
ocar.challenge: Prior tracking was slow and inaccurate, and a single microtubule can run far in-plane, so naive candidates and orientation priors miss or fragment tracks.
ocar.action: Eckstein, Buhmann, Cook, and Funke, at MICCAI (2020), predict microtubule scores with a 3D UNet, build a candidate graph via strided NMS, and select tracks with a new integer linear program plus block-wise distributed solving, benchmarked on CREMI Drosophila tissue.
ocar.resolution: On three 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm test volumes they report a 53% accuracy increase and three-order-of-magnitude speed-up versus prior art (NMS GRAD averaged over sets A, B, C). They release eight densely annotated 30 × 1000 × 1000 voxel blocks. Block-wise ILP is described as enabling petabyte-scale tracking without a significant accuracy drop.
ocar.future_work: Ablations show connected-component candidates are worse and swapping the UNet for a random forest with NMS causes many false positives; noisy scores still hurt precision when NMS over-extracts candidates.

summaries.beginner: Tiny tubes inside neurons are visible in electron-microscope pictures and can help check whether a cell was traced correctly. This paper teaches a computer to follow those tubes much faster and more accurately than earlier software.
summaries.intermediate: Presented at MICCAI (2020; arXiv:2009.08371), Eckstein and colleagues track microtubules in EM by UNet scoring, strided non-maximum suppression candidates, and a new ILP with biological structural priors. On three 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm Drosophila volumes they report 53% higher accuracy and ~1000× speed-up versus prior art. A block-wise scheme supports distributed tracking. They release eight annotated 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm CREMI blocks (github.com/nilsec/micron). Qualitative results include calyx reconstruction in a 76 × 52 × 64 µm Drosophila region in the supplement.
summaries.advanced: The 53% figure is an average over test sets A–B–C for NMS GRAD; NMS SM wins on B and C. Accuracy metric details live in Table 1, not fully reproduced here. CREMI blocks are small relative to whole-brain EM. Microtubule tracks are proposed as proofreading aids, not demonstrated to reduce neuron-split/merge error in this extract.

plain_language_summary: Tiny tubes inside neurons are visible in electron-microscope pictures and can help check whether a cell was traced correctly. This paper teaches a computer to follow those tubes much faster and more accurately than earlier software.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM must choose between large fields of view at limited z-resolution (ATUM/ssTEM) and isotropic FIB-SEM in small volumes; rare events need both context and local isotropic detail.
ocar.challenge: Ultramicrotomy z-thickness and FIB-SEM volume limits are in tension, especially when the target (for example microglia–plaque contacts) is sparse.
ocar.action: Kislinger, Gnägi, Kerschensteiner, Simons, Misgeld, and Schifferer, in iScience (2020), cut 2–10 µm resin sections onto transparent tape, map them by light and EM, then mill selected regions with FIB-SEM (ATUM-FIB), demonstrated on microglia–amyloid contacts in a familial Alzheimer’s mouse model.
ocar.resolution: Serial semithick sections act as a tissue library for on-demand isotropic ultrastructure after relocation of preselected structures. Highlights include fast nanometer-resolution relocation and tape-based multiscale LM/EM.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include sample-specific embedding, fracture risk at contrast transitions, and the method not being optimized to minimize material loss between sections for dense connectomic reconstruction (unlike ultrathick partitioning).

summaries.beginner: Researchers often must choose between seeing a large piece of tissue coarsely or a tiny piece in fine 3D. This hybrid method slices the tissue into thick-ish sheets, finds the rare spot of interest, then zooms in with ion-beam electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: Published in iScience (2020), Kislinger and colleagues introduce ATUM-FIB: serial 2–10 µm resin sections collected on transparent tape, mapped by serial light and electron microscopy, then targeted with FIB-SEM. They use the section library to locate microglia contact sites with amyloid plaques in a mouse model of familial Alzheimer’s disease. The method aims at isotropic local ultrastructure with surrounding microscopic context. Catalog metadata list bioRxiv; the PDF is the iScience article (DOI 10.1016/j.isci.2020.101290).
summaries.advanced: Authors state ATUM-FIB is for targeted structures, not dense large-scale connectomics, because material loss between semithick sections is not minimized. Embedding and contrasting must be retuned per sample; gray–white transitions are fracture-prone. Datasets were not in a public repository at publication (available on request). Voxel sizes and plaque-contact counts are not in the selected extract.

plain_language_summary: Researchers often must choose between seeing a large piece of tissue coarsely or a tiny piece in fine 3D. This hybrid method slices the tissue into thick-ish sheets, finds the rare spot of interest, then zooms in with ion-beam electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: A connectome is a comprehensive network map of neural elements and their links, and the concept now organizes structural and functional human brain research.
ocar.challenge: Maps can refer to neurons or areas and to synapses or pathways, so definitions, topology, dynamics, and clinical individual differences need a single conceptual frame.
ocar.action: Sporns, in the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (2020), surveys origins and definitions of the connectome, major findings on human connectome topology and how structure shapes dynamics, and themes in development and clinical populations.
ocar.resolution: At a given scale, connectome maps are presented as a complete, systematic account of anatomical or physiological relationships used to study both typical organization and individual differences.
ocar.future_work: The chapter is an overview; it points to ongoing work on individual differences rather than a new dataset.

summaries.beginner: A connectome is a map of how parts of the nervous system are linked, whether those parts are single cells or whole brain areas. This textbook chapter explains the idea and how it is used in human brain research.
summaries.intermediate: In the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (2020), Sporns reviews the connectome concept: neural elements (neurons or areas) and their interconnections (synapses or pathways). The chapter covers structural versus functional connectivity, topology of the human connectome, how connectivity shapes dynamics, and selected themes in development and clinical populations. It emphasizes complete, systematic maps at a chosen scale.
summaries.advanced: The associated PDF extract is a different paper: Riley et al., Imaging Neuroscience (2026), on Wasserstein distances and a CRAM pipeline for functional-connectome fingerprinting and phenotype prediction, not Sporns’s textbook chapter. This card uses only the catalog abstract. The chapter is pedagogical survey, not original graph-theoretic results.

plain_language_summary: A connectome is a map of how parts of the nervous system are linked, whether those parts are single cells or whole brain areas. This textbook chapter explains the idea and how it is used in human brain research.

ocar.opportunity: Segmented EM and other volumes store nominal IDs, so ordinary mipmaps and volume rendering alias badly; a compact structure that preserves label mixtures would allow interactive viewing and queries.
ocar.challenge: Each coarse voxel holds a mixture of segment IDs; naively storing and range-querying those histograms is expensive, and transfer functions plus lighting must stay consistent across scales.
ocar.action: Al-Thelaya, Agus, and Schneider, in IEEE TVCG (IEEE Vis 2020), factor mixtures into sequences of two-label interpolations, store them as a pruned DAG (the Mixture Graph), propagate transfer functions from leaves, and support footprint histogram queries.
ocar.resolution: The structure compresses histogram mipmaps, enables pre-filtered rendering at interactive rates, and yields up to 178× speed-up over naive parallelized range queries. Applications include pre-filtered lighting and multi-dimensional transfer functions for shape, geometry, and orientation. Example volumes include hippocampus (1178×1125×789, 353 segments), neocortex (2048×2048×300, 1,182 segments), and a fiber-reinforced polymer (15,917 segments).
ocar.future_work: The extract’s back matter is references; remaining limits on extreme label counts or out-of-core volumes are not detailed in the selected text.

summaries.beginner: When a 3D scan is labeled with many cell IDs, zooming out mixes those labels and the picture can flicker or lie. This data structure stores those mixes compactly so you can still render and ask “what labels are in this box?” quickly.
summaries.intermediate: To appear in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (IEEE Vis 2020; arXiv:2009.02702), Al-Thelaya, Agus, and Schneider introduce the Mixture Graph for segmentation-histogram mipmaps. Mixtures are factored into linear interpolations between exactly two IDs and stored as a topologically ordered DAG after pruning. Transfer functions propagate from sources for pre-filtered rendering; footprint queries of partial histograms reach up to 178× versus naive parallel range queries. They also show pre-filtered lighting and interactive exploration with multi-dimensional transfer functions.
summaries.advanced: The 178× figure is an upper bound stated in the abstract, not a per-volume table here. Example volumes mix connectomic (hippocampus, neocortex) and materials data. Novelty is the histogram/DAG factorization, not a new segmentation algorithm. Catalog hyphenation “The Mixture Graph-A Data Structure” matches the title.

plain_language_summary: When a 3D scan is labeled with many cell IDs, zooming out mixes those labels and the picture can flicker or lie. This data structure stores those mixes compactly so you can still render and ask “what labels are in this box?” quickly.

ocar.opportunity: Whole-brain Drosophila connectomes will sit on decades of circuit genetics, offering a path to entire-brain function rather than isolated pathways.
ocar.challenge: In a complete wiring diagram, sensory channels are synaptically interconnected even at early layers, and higher brain regions are densely linked by long-range projections, so contributions of “distinct” circuits are hard to isolate; extrasynaptic communication also matters.
ocar.action: Vogt, in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), perspectives upcoming larval and adult Drosophila whole-brain reconstructions at Janelia in light of the C. elegans precedent (302 neurons) and argues for combining connectomics with genetic tools and behavior.
ocar.resolution: Connectomes are framed as a scaffold for existing circuit knowledge, while warning that whole-brain context undermines clean isolation of sensory versus higher systems and that modulation beyond direct synapses must be included.
ocar.future_work: The piece looks ahead to using fly genetics and behavioral paradigms on whole-brain maps rather than reporting a finished fly connectome.

summaries.beginner: Complete fruit-fly brain wiring diagrams were on the way, building on the worm’s famous map. This perspective says those maps will help, but they will also show that brain parts are more mixed together than textbook circuits suggest.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), Vogt discusses the coming larval and adult Drosophila whole-brain connectomes from Janelia, following C. elegans as the first complete synaptic map. The essay argues that whole-brain wiring reveals early sensory cross-talk, dense long-range higher-brain projections, and convergence centers, so circuit isolation is difficult. It also stresses communication beyond direct synapses. Drosophila genetics and behavior are presented as the way to pursue entire-brain function on that scaffold.
summaries.advanced: The associated PDF extract is a different paper: Gajardo, Guerra, and Campusano, International Journal of Molecular Sciences (2023), a review of serotonergic modulation of Drosophila spatial navigation, not Vogt’s connectome perspective. This card uses only the catalog abstract. Janelia whole-brain reconstructions are prospective in the 2020 text.

plain_language_summary: Complete fruit-fly brain wiring diagrams were on the way, building on the worm’s famous map. This perspective says those maps will help, but they will also show that brain parts are more mixed together than textbook circuits suggest.

ocar.opportunity: Tract-tracing metastudies build connectome databases by hand, so measuring how much experts disagree would show whether adjacency matrices are trustworthy.
ocar.challenge: Tracing papers are often non-standardized, so different experts may extract different connections from the same article, with unknown effects on graph analyses.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, Schwanke, Lessmann, Meinhardt, Beier, Kadir, Karnitzki, Sellner, Klünker, Ruß, and Jenssen, in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2019), have three blinded experts extract hypothalamic connections from 16 tract-tracing papers and propose a workflow to detect variability across processing steps.
ocar.resolution: Inter-rater variability was found; they analyze observation scores, matrix visualizations of discrepant connections, and weight variation in adjacency matrices. Data and software are pointed to neuroviisas.med.uni-rostock.de.
ocar.future_work: The hypothalamus sample is presented as an example; the workflow is meant for broader connectome metastudies.

summaries.beginner: When scientists copy wiring information out of old tracing papers, they may not all copy the same links. This study has several experts read the same hypothalamus papers and measures how much their connection lists disagree.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Briefings in Bioinformatics (2019), Schmitt and colleagues quantify inter-rater and inter-observation variability in tract-tracing-based hypothalamic connectivity. Three blinded experts extracted connections from 16 publications. A workflow flags variability at multiple processing steps, with observation scores, discrepancy matrices, and adjacency-weight variation. Resources are at the neuroVIISAS site.
summaries.advanced: The associated PDF extract is a different paper: Schmitt, Eipert, Wang, Kanoke, Rabiller, and Liu, bioRxiv (2023), on connectome-based prediction of functional impairment in three experimental rat stroke models using neuroVIISAS, not the 2019 hypothalamic inter-rater study. This card uses only the catalog abstract. No numeric agreement coefficients appear in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When scientists copy wiring information out of old tracing papers, they may not all copy the same links. This study has several experts read the same hypothalamus papers and measures how much their connection lists disagree.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uniquely combines a complete connectome, a well-characterized genome, and quantifiable behavior, so an integrated systems description from genes to locomotion is conceivable.
ocar.challenge: Reverse engineering still requires perturbations and models that cross molecular, circuit, and behavioral scales; even with 302 neurons, structure does not automatically yield function.
ocar.action: Karbowski, in Current Opinion in Systems Biology (2019; arXiv:1910.07451), reviews computational and perturbation work on worm circuits, emphasizing locomotion, and sketches phenomenological multi-state velocity models that can be taken to a Fokker–Planck limit.
ocar.resolution: The review collects successes and challenges of merging genomics, connectomics, behavior, and modeling. An appendix-like derivation relates discrete forward/backward/stop states to continuous noisy velocity dynamics whose drift and diffusion could, in principle, be measured to constrain transition rates.
ocar.future_work: Measuring A(v) and B(v) experimentally is proposed as a way to identify rates in the phenomenological model; it is not carried out here.

summaries.beginner: The worm is the only animal with a full wiring diagram, a mapped genome, and simple measurable behaviors. This review asks how far computer models and genetic or cell perturbations have gone toward explaining how that animal moves.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Current Opinion in Systems Biology (2019; arXiv preprint 1910.07451), Karbowski reviews systems-level C. elegans work with a computational emphasis. He argues the worm uniquely spans genome, 302-neuron connectome, and quantifiable behavior, unlike rodents or flies that still lack complete neuron-to-neuron diagrams. The selected extract includes a phenomenological locomotion model (forward, backward, stop, and a 2N+1 velocity-state extension) reduced to a Fokker–Planck equation for velocity.
summaries.advanced: This is a review plus a modeling sketch, not new connectome data. The Fokker–Planck reduction is theoretical; A(v) and B(v) are not measured here. Comparisons to rodent and fly structure–function studies are qualitative. Catalog LaTeX in the abstract ({\it Caenorhabditis elegans}) is source formatting.

plain_language_summary: The worm is the only animal with a full wiring diagram, a mapped genome, and simple measurable behaviors. This review asks how far computer models and genetic or cell perturbations have gone toward explaining how that animal moves.

ocar.opportunity: Human brain connectomes are common, but a draft spinal cord connectome could template simulations of pain, stimulation, and other spinal computations.
ocar.challenge: Human cell counts and connections are incompletely measured, so the draft must mix human histology with other species’ data and still be calibrated before it makes testable predictions.
ocar.action: Arle, Iftimia, Shils, Mei, and Carlson, in Neural Computation (2019), compile cell types, connectivity, and strengths from the literature, estimate neuron numbers from cadaveric measurements and histology, and simulate circuitry across all ten Rexed laminae in 31 segments, including a study of spinal cord stimulation for analgesia.
ocar.resolution: The model includes intra- and interlaminar, intersegmental, and ascending/descending connections, estimated counts per cell type, and highly recurrent local networks. It is offered as a starting point for biomedical hypotheses, each needing extra calibration.
ocar.future_work: The authors call for simulating additional segments and expanding research uses; each application requires further constraints on outputs.

summaries.beginner: Most wiring maps are of the brain, not the spinal cord. This paper builds a first-draft computer model of human spinal circuits from published anatomy and uses it to think about spinal stimulation for pain.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Neural Computation (2019), Arle and colleagues construct a draft human spinal cord connectome from literature on cell types, connectivity, and strengths, using other species where human data are missing. Neuron counts are estimated from cadaveric measurements, cross-sectional histology, and cytoarchitecture. Simulations cover ten Rexed laminae in all 31 segments with intra-, inter-laminar, intersegmental, and brain connections, and include a study of spinal cord stimulation for analgesia. Highly interconnected recurrent networks are noted.
summaries.advanced: The associated PDF extract is a different paper: Nasirinezhad et al., Basic and Clinical Neuroscience (2021), an open-label bumetanide trial for neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury (9 of 14 completers), not Arle’s computational connectome. This card uses only the catalog abstract. Neuron counts are estimates; the model is a draft requiring application-specific calibration.

plain_language_summary: Most wiring maps are of the brain, not the spinal cord. This paper builds a first-draft computer model of human spinal circuits from published anatomy and uses it to think about spinal stimulation for pain.

ocar.opportunity: Collecting ultrathin sections on silicon wafers enables post-staining and volumetric CLEM, but manual collection is skilled, slow, and unreliable, while tape methods pack poorly and can block fluorescence.
ocar.challenge: Destructive block-face methods forbid reimaging and wet stains; ATUM tape has low packing density, autofluorescence or scratches, and extra handling; knife-to-wafer ribbons demand constant monitoring.
ocar.action: Templier, in eLife (2019), glues superparamagnetic nanoparticle resin onto polymerized sample blocks (MagC) so hundreds of sections can be remotely actuated and collected at high density on wafers, demonstrated with neuroanatomical tracers in zebra finch HVC.
ocar.resolution: MagC collected hundreds of serial ultrathin sections directly on silicon for correlative visualization of tracers in volumetric EM. The conclusion expects use beyond connectomics and, with ion-beam milling and multibeam EM, as a platform for large-volume EM.
ocar.future_work: Animal work used two zebra finches with tracer injections into HVC; broader species and fully automated multibeam pipelines are prospective.

summaries.beginner: Picking up thousands of extremely thin tissue slices by hand is slow and easy to ruin. This method adds a magnetic bit of plastic so a magnet can gather the slices onto a wafer for both light and electron microscopy.
summaries.intermediate: Published in eLife (2019; catalog metadata also list bioRxiv), Templier introduces MagC: a magnetic resin on the sample block enables remote collection of hundreds of ultrathin sections at high packing density on silicon wafers, avoiding tape autofluorescence and low density. The method supported volumetric CLEM of neuroanatomical tracers in zebra finch HVC after perfusion and 150 µm vibratome slices. Catalog abstract emphasizes post-embedding staining and correlative tracer visualization. The conclusion points to combination with broad or gas-cluster ion milling and multibeam EM.
summaries.advanced: “Hundreds of sections” is not a single reported yield with error bars in the selected text. Demonstration is tracer CLEM in songbird HVC, not a dense mammalian connectome. Competing-interest and funding live on later pages. Catalog journal field says bioRxiv; the PDF is the eLife paper (10.7554/eLife.45696).

plain_language_summary: Picking up thousands of extremely thin tissue slices by hand is slow and easy to ruin. This method adds a magnetic bit of plastic so a magnet can gather the slices onto a wafer for both light and electron microscopy.

ocar.opportunity: EM maps synapses but rarely cell type; multiplexed genetic labels compatible with standard EM would let defined populations be distinguished in one volume.
ocar.challenge: Light microscopy multiplexes easily; EM has lacked a practical multiplex system. Immuno-gold needs special prep that harms ultrastructure, and spectral EM methods need specialized equipment.
ocar.action: Zhang, Lee, Paul, and Ginty, in Nature Neuroscience (2019), develop dAPEX2 reporters targeted to different subcellular compartments—15 AAV constructs and six mouse lines—and show double and triple labeling of primary afferents, cortical descending inputs, and inhibitory interneurons in spinal dorsal horn.
ocar.resolution: dAPEX2 gives stronger signal than prior ascorbate peroxidases and is compatible with existing EM pipelines without spectral separation. Tools were deposited in public repositories. Proof-of-principle experiments demonstrated synaptic connections among the labeled populations.
ocar.future_work: The discussion presents the toolkit for complex mammalian neuropils; scale-up to large volume EM and more than three simultaneous labels is implied rather than fully benchmarked in the extract.

summaries.beginner: Electron microscopy shows synapses clearly but usually cannot tell which genetic cell types they belong to. This team stains different cell classes with a darker enzyme targeted to different parts of the cell so several types can be seen at once.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Neuroscience (2019), Zhang and colleagues introduce multiplexed peroxidase EM labeling based on dAPEX2, with 15 AAV constructs and six mouse reporter lines targeting distinct subcellular compartments. The protocol is described as compatible with existing EM pipelines. Double and triple labeling in spinal cord dorsal horn showed synapses among primary afferents, descending cortical inputs, and inhibitory interneurons. The discussion contrasts this with immuno-gold (epitope loss, poor ultrastructure) and energy-filtered TEM (specialized hardware).
summaries.advanced: Improved signal versus prior APEX tools is qualitative in the abstract (“dramatically improved”). Proof-of-principle is spinal dorsal horn, not brain-wide. Multiplexing relies on compartment location, not color, so crowded neuropil could still confuse labels if compartments overlap. Quantification of the EM volume is mentioned in author contributions but not numbered in the extract.

plain_language_summary: Electron microscopy shows synapses clearly but usually cannot tell which genetic cell types they belong to. This team stains different cell classes with a darker enzyme targeted to different parts of the cell so several types can be seen at once.

ocar.opportunity: The 1986 C. elegans connectome made structural wiring a starting point for behavior, but function also depends on activity, development, extrasynaptic signals, and models.
ocar.challenge: Structural connectivity does not by itself predict whole-organism behavior; gap junctions and extrasynaptic signaling sit outside the chemical-synapse matrix.
ocar.action: DiLoreto, Chute, Bryce, and Srinivasan, in Journal of Developmental Biology (2019), review technologies for whole-organism functional connectomics—calcium imaging, optogenetics, sonogenetics, multisensory integration—plus developmental lineage and computational network models.
ocar.resolution: They argue that combining perturbation tools with models of single-cell biophysics and whole-network dynamics is required to go from wiring to sensory-to-motor behavior. Both hermaphrodite (302) and male (385) nervous systems are noted as fully mapped at EM level.
ocar.future_work: The review expects functional connectomics to expand with large brain initiatives and calls for frameworks that span scales; it does not present a new whole-worm activity map.

summaries.beginner: We know every synapse in the worm, but that still does not tell us how it behaves. This review covers tools that watch, turn on, or turn off cells in the living animal, and computer models that try to put those measurements together.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Journal of Developmental Biology (2019), DiLoreto and colleagues review functional connectomics in C. elegans after the 1986 structural map. Topics include linking activity to behavior and sensory input, developmental origins of connectivity, and computational models of neurons and networks. Keywords highlight calcium imaging, optogenetics, sonogenetics, and multi-sensory integration. The introduction notes that gap junctions and extrasynaptic signaling mean the chemical connectome is not the whole functional story.
summaries.advanced: This is a technology review, not a new connectome. Neuron counts 302/385 are standard citations. Whether structure defines function is posed as an open mindset split, not settled. Closing remarks on the Human Connectome Project, BRAIN, and HBP are contextual, not worm results.

plain_language_summary: We know every synapse in the worm, but that still does not tell us how it behaves. This review covers tools that watch, turn on, or turn off cells in the living animal, and computer models that try to put those measurements together.

ocar.opportunity: Axonal arbor shape is a cell-type descriptor and routes long-range information, but few mouse projection neurons had been reconstructed in full.
ocar.challenge: Thin axons (~100 nm) travel centimeters across regions, so serial-section tracing has historically yielded small, often partial samples and bulk tracers average over types.
ocar.action: Winnubst, Bas, Ferreira, Wu, Economo, and colleagues, on bioRxiv (2019), present a MouseLight imaging and reconstruction platform and reconstruct more than 1,000 projection neurons in motor cortex, thalamus, subiculum, and hypothalamus, totaling more than 75 meters of axon, in a searchable database (mouselight.janelia.org).
ocar.resolution: Complete morphologies revealed previously unknown projection subtypes and organizational principles of long-range connectivity, including clustering into putative types, subtypes within known classes, and topographic gradients of single-cell projections.
ocar.future_work: The discussion contrasts this with bulk anterograde studies and combinatorial retrograde labeling whose injection counts scale poorly with target number; expanding coverage beyond the sampled regions is implied.

summaries.beginner: A neuron’s long-distance cable can wander through much of the mouse brain, but those cables are rarely traced from end to end. This project images and draws more than a thousand complete cells and puts them in an online atlas.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (2019), Winnubst and colleagues describe a platform for complete mouse projection-neuron morphologies, including axons spanning large fractions of the brain. They report more than 1,000 reconstructions in motor cortex, thalamus, subiculum, and hypothalamus, together exceeding 75 meters of axonal length, at mouselight.janelia.org. Clustering of axonal shapes identified putative cell types, subtypes within known projection classes, and topographic gradients. The discussion argues bulk labeling averages away idiosyncratic single-axon organization.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2019 preprint of the MouseLight resource; later journal versions may differ. “Previously unknown subtypes” are clustering-derived and should be checked against the figures. Axon diameter ~100 nm is cited from literature. The extract does not give per-region cell counts or error rates for automated tracing. EM synapses are not mapped; this is light-microscopy morphology.

plain_language_summary: A neuron’s long-distance cable can wander through much of the mouse brain, but those cables are rarely traced from end to end. This project images and draws more than a thousand complete cells and puts them in an online atlas.

ocar.opportunity: Comparing spectral properties of structural connectomes across organisms could show what, if anything, is distinctive about human brain networks and speak to the brain-criticality debate.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear which organizational features matter for cognition and which evolutionary wiring rules produce observed graphs; human networks may not follow the same growth heuristics as other animals.
ocar.action: Anokhin, Avetisov, Gorsky, Nechaev, Pospelov, and Valba (Physics of Life Reviews, 2019; arXiv:1812.06317) perform comparative spectral analysis of open-access structural connectomes and study graph-Laplacian level spacing.
ocar.resolution: Human spectral density showed the largest deviation from a randomized network among organisms studied. Preference for 3-cycle formation reproduced many animal connectomes but fitting the human graph required conserving local clustering. Laplacian level spacing matched a hybrid Wigner–Dyson/Poisson critical regime familiar in condensed-matter physics, taken as support for brain criticality.
ocar.future_work: The work frames spectral criticality as evidence in a debate rather than a mechanistic model of cognition; linking spectra to function is left open.

summaries.beginner: Researchers compared the “sound” of brain-network graphs across animals by looking at their mathematical spectra. The human map stood out, and its spacing of graph frequencies looked like a physical system sitting at a critical point.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Physics of Life Reviews (2019; arXiv:1812.06317), Pospelov and coauthors compare structural-connectome spectra across organisms using open-access data. Human spectral density deviated most from randomized nulls. A 3-cycle-preferring evolutionary model fitted many animal connectomes; human fits required conserving local clustering. They report the first level-spacing analysis of the human connectome graph Laplacian, matching a critical Wigner–Dyson/Poisson hybrid. Authors interpret this as support for brain criticality.
summaries.advanced: Connectomes are structural graphs at the parcellation of each open dataset, not synaptic EM maps. “Maximal deviation” is comparative, without the numeric scores in the extract. Criticality is an interpretation of spectral statistics, not a demonstration of neural avalanches. Catalog author list is duplicated; the arXiv byline is Anokhin, Avetisov, Gorsky, Nechaev, Pospelov, Valba.

plain_language_summary: Researchers compared the “sound” of brain-network graphs across animals by looking at their mathematical spectra. The human map stood out, and its spacing of graph frequencies looked like a physical system sitting at a critical point.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks segment large biomedical images well, but labs are blocked by software environments and scarce GPU clusters.
ocar.challenge: Even strong architectures for 2D/3D EM, X-ray, and light microscopy remain inaccessible if users cannot reproduce Caffe-style pipelines or obtain compute.
ocar.action: Haberl, Churas, Tindall, Boassa, Phan, Bushong, Madany, Akay, Deerinck, Peltier, and Ellisman, in Nature Methods (2018; bioRxiv 353425), release CDeep3M, a cloud CNN on Amazon Web Services with instructions to train and apply it on large 2D and 3D microscopy datasets.
ocar.resolution: They benchmark on complex light, X-ray, and electron microscopy segmentation tasks and present CDeep3M as a plug-and-play, publicly available cloud solution so labs need not build local high-performance stacks.
ocar.future_work: Generalized applicability still depends on user-provided training labels for new modalities; the extract’s main text stresses access more than a single accuracy number.

summaries.beginner: Powerful image-segmentation networks often stay locked in expert labs because the software is hard to install. This team puts a ready-made deep-learning segmenter in the cloud so other groups can train it on their microscope pictures.
summaries.intermediate: Published in Nature Methods (2018), with a matching bioRxiv preprint in the extract, Haberl and colleagues present CDeep3M, a pre-configured cloud deep convolutional network on AWS for 2D and 3D biomedical segmentation. They address environment and compute bottlenecks and benchmark on large, complex light, X-ray, and electron microscopy datasets. The Nature Methods abstract frames it as a user-friendly cloud tool; the preprint abstract emphasizes simple training instructions for diverse modalities.
summaries.advanced: The selected PDF is the bioRxiv preprint of the Nature Methods paper (same authors and title family), not a different study. Numeric benchmark scores are not in the selected extract (discussion not captured). Cloud credits from an NIH pilot are acknowledged. “Plug-and-play” still requires training data for new tasks.

plain_language_summary: Powerful image-segmentation networks often stay locked in expert labs because the software is hard to install. This team puts a ready-made deep-learning segmenter in the cloud so other groups can train it on their microscope pictures.

ocar.opportunity: Fully supervised encoder–decoder CNNs segment volume EM well but need many pixel labels; domain adaptation could reuse existing ground truth on new microscopes or preparations.
ocar.challenge: Most DA methods are for classification; features from one EM domain often fail on another (brain versus HeLa, isotropic FIB/SEM versus anisotropic TEM).
ocar.action: Roels, Hennies, Saeys, Philips, and Kreshuk (ISBI 2019; arXiv:1810.09734) extend classification DA to encoder–decoders and add a reconstruction decoder that aligns source and target encoder features, tested on mitochondria segmentation.
ocar.resolution: DA from brain EM to HeLa cells and from isotropic FIB/SEM to anisotropic TEM outperformed extended classification DA methods and a finetuning baseline. Code is at github.com/JorisRoels/domain-adaptive-segmentation. Future work mentioned includes unsupervised/zero-shot segmentation DA.
ocar.future_work: Zero-shot and fully unsupervised DA for volume EM segmentation are explicitly left for later work.

summaries.beginner: A computer trained to outline mitochondria in one kind of electron-microscope image often fails on another lab’s images. This paper adds a reconstruction task so the network learns features that transfer, needing fewer new hand labels.
summaries.intermediate: Presented at IEEE ISBI (2019; arXiv:1810.09734), Roels and colleagues adapt domain-adaptation methods to encoder–decoder EM segmentation and propose an extra reconstruction decoder to align source and target features. Tasks are mitochondria segmentation: brain EM to HeLa cells, and isotropic FIB/SEM to anisotropic TEM. In all cases the method beat extended classification DA techniques and finetuning. An implementation is released on GitHub.
summaries.advanced: The extract does not include numeric IoU/F1 tables. Success is claimed on mitochondria, not neuron membranes or synapses. Source/target dataset names beyond brain/HeLa and FIB/SEM versus TEM are in the abstract. Catalog year is 2018; the ISBI DOI is 2019. Unsupervised zero-shot DA is proposed, not evaluated here.
